words.intro: A German wedding takes place twice: first at the registry office, by law, on a weekday, in a room with a plant. The party comes later. Between them, there’s plenty of time to wonder what you’ve done.

document.intro: A real sign, in the green, outside a town hall in Schleswig-Holstein. In a small town the town hall is also the registry office. There’s no need to read the small print. Use the sign to write your wishes about the past.
document.fact: Couples in Germany need to register their wedding at the *Standesamt* in advance, sometimes months ahead for popular dates. Any date that reads well, such as 12.12.12, fills up at once.

reading.title: Polterabend
reading.intro: Remember the bride who lost her shoe in Cologne? She’s Sophie, and she and Max are getting married, at last. The night before a wedding, by old custom, friends smash plates on the doorstep and the couple sweep up. It’s very late, and there is a lot to sweep. Max is thinking.
reading.photos[1].caption: Der gedeckte Tisch: Alles ist gut, solange niemand eine Rede hält.
reading.fact: At a *Polterabend*, the evening before the wedding, friends break china (never glass, which means bad luck) on the doorstep, and the couple must clean it up together. Only the legal ceremony at the *Standesamt* makes you married. The church is optional, and it comes afterwards.
